Prevention of obesity #1

Slide 2 #2

Slide 3 #3

  • “The most cost-effective initiatives are likely to be population wide and use integrated, multi-disciplinary, comprehensive and sustainable
  • approaches, involving a wide variety of complementary actions which address the individual, community, the environment, and society at large.”
  • IASO Policy Briefing The prevention of obesity and NCDs: Challenges and opportunities for governments . January 2014
  • Individual level – personalized intervention
  • global risk reduction
  • weight reduction
  • (re)weight gain prevention

Slide 4 #4

  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Division of Nutrition, Physical Activity, and Obesity, 2008
  • Prevention

Important periods for obesity prevention #5

  • Pregnancy
  • Childhood
  • Young adult
  • Postmenopausal

Slide 6 #6

  • The science shows that consuming a healthy dietary pattern, meeting food group and nutrient needs with nutrient-dense foods and beverages, and limiting intake of foods and beverages that are not nutrient-dense is related to many health benefits.
  • Science also supports the idea that every life stage provides an opportunity to make food choices that promote health and well-being, achieve and maintain appropriate weight status, and reduce risk of diet-related chronic disease.

Slide 7 #7

Slide 9 #9

Slide 10 #10

  • There is more and more evidence that children who gain weight rapidly during early life are at higher risk of obesity in later life
  • Three periods in early life may be particularly important for the development of obesity and its associated morbidity and mortality:
  • the perinatal period – first 6-12 months / 24 months
  • the period of adiposity rebound – 5-6 y
  • and puberty/adolescence.
  • In normal physiological circumstances, during the first year of life BMI increases rapidly, but then decreases, reaching a minimum usually ~5–6 years of age = minimum BMI = adiposity rebound
  • Critical and sensitive periods for the primary prevention of obesity

Does childhood obesity necessarily lead to adult obesity ? #11

  • The majority of longitudinal studies which tracked obesity from childhood to adulthood (18 – 36 years) found that fatter children are more likely (two- to four-fold) to become obese adults.
  • The risk for future adulthood obesity increases constantly between age 1 – 2 years and 15 – 17 years.
  • The current scientific perception is that the number of adipocytes is mostly set during childhood and adolescence.
  • Michal Efrat et al. J Pediatr Endocr Met 2013; 26(3-4): 197–209

Slide 12 #12

  • The total adipocyte number increases in childhood and adolescence and remains constant in adult life in both lean and obese individuals
  • Attempts to slow down fat cell multiplication during childhood should prevent adult obesity.
  • Risk factors for obesity:
  • High birth weight
  • Low birth weight = ” predisposition to gain weight rapidly during the first 2 years of postnatal life “ catch-up ”
  • Young adults with an early rebound ( age of 5 – 5.5 y) have 2 – 5 higher BMI values in their 20s than those with a late rebound
  • Michal Efrat et al. J Pediatr Endocr Met 2013; 26(3-4): 197–209
  • Does childhood obesity necessarily lead to adult obesity ?

Slide 13 #13

Slide 14 #14

  • Adolescence offers a therapeutic window with a unique opportunity to modify the risk of future obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease and achieve long-term prevention

Slide 15 #15

  • Adolescence is characterized by changes in quantity and location of body fat, which is part of the reason that it is a critical period for abnormal weight gain.
  • Early adolescence is associated with a substantial increase in adipocyte (fat cell) size and number.
  • A. S. Alberga et al. Pediatr Obes
  • . 2012 Aug;7(4):261-73

Curr Obes Rep. Published online 26 Jan 2016 #16

  • Conclusion
  • It is clear that young adults demonstrate some dietary behaviors that place them at risk of weight gain.
  • Individual foods and beverages with high saturated fat, sugar and sodium contents and of high-energy density such as those purchased at quick service restaurants feature prominently in diets of young adults in many countries including the USA, UK, and Australia.
  • Continued poor intakes of fruit and vegetables might further increase the risk of chronic disease.

Dietary Practices that Might Give Rise to Weight Gain #17

  • Meal Skipping
  • Snacking Between Meals
  • Portion Size
  • Cooking Skills : “art of cooking has been lost in the young”
  • Curr Obes Rep. Published online 26 Jan 2016

“Healthy Eating and Active Lifestyles Begin at Home” #18

  • Encourage healthy eating habits in young children by providing a variety of
  • nutritious foods, limiting junk food and sugary drinks, and encouraging
  • parents to do the same at home:
  • • Offer a mix of different colored vegetables each day, especially dark green and red and orange vegetables
  • • Variety of whole fruits, rather than juice
  • All breads, cereals, and pastas served are whole grain
  • Heart-healthy lean protein
  • Healthy monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fats like olive
  • Mealtimes enjoyable and television-free
  • Allow children to eat to their own fullness without pressure to overeat
  • Avoid the use of food as a reward or punishment
  • Center for Disease Control and Prevention

“Healthy Eating and Active Lifestyles Begin at Home” #19

  • Being active, not sitting or watching television
  • Ensure that children of all ages are not sitting longer than 15- to 30-minute intervals, unless during meals or naptime
  • Limit any media viewing (television, cell phone, or digital media) in the child care setting to no more than 30 minutes per week for children age 2 and older

Slide 20 #20

  • Weight gain during pregnancy, and post-partum weight retention, may be an important predictor of the mothers’ risk of subsequent obesity and diabetes.

Intrauterine over-nutrition predicts life long obesity #21

  • Obese mothers are 4 X more likely to have obese children;
  • The risk rises to over 10 X if the father is also obese.
  • Driven by genetic or behavioral factors, much of this risk is due to excess childhood weight gain.
  • Insufficient fetal nutrition can also be a risk factor for obesity.
  • Maternal smoking during pregnancy has been associated with increased risk of later obesity due to rapid postnatal catch-up growth
  • Pregnancy
  • International Journal of Epidemiology 2006;35:3–9

Healthy lifestyle..... #22

Hypoglycemia is relatively rare in people without diabetes. #23

  • Whipple’s triad sets the diagnosis, and its documentation is obligatory for the beginning of investigation for determining the cause.
  • Whipple’s triad:
  • Signs/Symptoms of hypoglycemia
  • Glycemia < 55 mg/dL
  • Remission of symptoms upon glucose blood levels normalisation
  • Non-diabetic Hypoglycemia

Slide 24 #24

Tumors Extrapancreatic tumors – producing IGF-2 (Insulin-like growth factor 2) #25

  • Causes of Hypoglycemia
  • Nondiabetic patient
  • Insulinoma
  • Tumor localized in pancreas
  • Freq are benign
  • high insulin levels
  • high C peptide level

Causes of Hypoglycemia #26

  • Neonatal hypoglycemia
  • 1) Transient Neonatal Hypoglycemia
  • - resolves in 3-5 days
  • - premature,
  • - smaller of twins,
  • - respiratory distress,
  • -sepsis,
  • - large birth weight infants (e.g. infant of diabetic mother- hyperinsulinemia from islet cell hyperplasia)

Causes of Hypoglycemia #27

  • Neonatal hypoglycemia
  • 2)Persistent (recurrent) hypoglycemia
  • - does not resolve within 5-7 days
  • - Hormone deficiencies : GH deficiency, Cortisol insufficiency
  • - Hormone excess (hyperinsulinemia)
  • B cell hyperplasia (neisidioblastosis)
  • B cell adenoma
  • Beckwith-Weideman syndrome (Macrosomia, Macroglossia, Microcephaly, ear-lobe fissures)
  • - Metabolic diseases (inborn errors of metabolism)

Laboratory Diagnosis #28

  • Lab values must be obtained when the patient actually is hypoglycemic
  • Glycemia
  • C-peptide
  • Insulinemia
  • Insulin/glucose > 0.3
  • Fasting test 24-72 h

Insulinoma #29

  • Diagnosis:
  • Biochemical
  • Localization:
  • CT Scan
  • Octreoscan (scintigraphy with radiolabeled somatostatin analog )
  • Endoscopic US
  • Intraoperator U/S – most sensitive test
  • selective intra-arterial calcium stimulation test

Slide 30 #30

Slide 31 #31

Slide 32 #32

Hypoglycemia Treatment #33

  • For mild to moderate hypoglycemia: 15-20 mg carbohydrates
  • Severe hypoglycemia: iv glucose and/or glucagon (sc)
  • Medication (e.g. steroids) rarely needed

Treatment of Hyperinsulinemia #34

  • Diazoxide
  • 10 – 25 mg / kg / day divided t.i.d.
  • Octreotide (Sandostatin)
  • 1 – 20 mcg / kg / day SQ divided t.i.d. or continuous infusion via insulin pump
  • Tumor removal

Hyperuricemia #35

Uric acid is the final product of purine metabolism #36

  • Normal Uric acid level
  • < 6 mg/dL women ; (0.36 mmol/L)
  • For men is < 7 mg/dL (0.42 mmol/L)
  • 2/3 of total body urate is produced endogenously
  • 1/3 - dietary purines intake
  • Approximately 70% of the urate produced daily is excreted by the kidneys, while the rest is eliminated by the intestines.
  • However, during renal failure, the intestinal contribution of urate excretion increases to compensate for the decreased elimination by the kidneys.
  • Hyperuricemia

Pathophysiology #37

Pathophysiology #38

Slide 39 #39

  • EpidemiologyThe prevalence of asymptomatic hyperuricemia in the general population is estimated at 2-13% (USA).
  • Mortality/Morbidity - Hyperuricemia
  • Associated
  • increased morbidity in patients with hypertension
  • increased mortality in women and elderly persons
  • modestly increase the risk of stroke incidence and mortality
  • is probably a marker for comorbid risk factors rather than a causative factor, per se.
  • Component of metabolic syndrome

Race #40

  • High prevalence of hyperuricemia - indigenous races of the Pacific
  • African American persons develop hyperuricemia more commonly than Caucasian persons
  • Gender
  • More common in men than in women.
  • Only 5% of patients with gout are female, but uric acid levels increase in women after menopause.
  • Age
  • Uric acid level is lower in children than in adults
  • The upper limit of the reference range for children is 5 mg/dL (0.30 mmol/L)
  • The tendency to develop hyperuricemia increases with age

Causes #41

  • Cardiovascular diseases
  • Obesity
  • Kidney failure
  • Alcohol, food excess (especially meat and organs)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Metabolic syndrome
  • Diuretic therapy, low-dose salicylate, cyclosporine, levodopa, nicotinic acid
  • Hypertension
  • Acidosis
  • Preeclampsia and eclampsia
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Hematologic malignancies, lead poisoning
  • Genetic

Clinical aspects #42

  • Asymptomatic hyperuricemia - no specific physical findings
  • Symptomatic
  • gout
  • urolithiasis

Clinical aspects #43

  • Gout – tipically manifests as an acute monoarthritis, recurrent episodes of painful inflammation of joints due to uric acid crystals deposit. Most commonly in the halux and less frequently in the tarsal joint, knee, and other joints.

Chronic tophaceous gouty artropathy #44

  • chronic arthritis involving one or more joints is another form of gout
  • associated with the formation of gouty tophi
  • “disease of Kings” : Charles Darwin, Benjamin Franklin, Martin Luther, King Henry VIII, Isaac Newton

Clinical aspects #45

  • Uric acid urolithiasis may manifest with hematuria, pain in the flank, abdomen, or inguinal region; and/or nausea and vomiting (renal colic).

Screening #46

  • Routine screening of hyperuricemia in the general population is not recommended.
  • It is only performed in:
  • persons with a family history of symptomatic or asymptomatic hyperuricemia
  • people with obesity, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure
  • Screening methods for hyperuricemia are:
  • serum uric acid (at least 14 days after the acute arthritis episode)

Diagnosis #47

  • Laboratory investigations
  • Serum uric acid
  • Complete blood count
  • Electrolytes, urea, serum creatinine:
  • abnormal in patients with acidosis or renal disease
  • Liver function tests
  • possible malignancy or metabolic disorders
  • Glycemia - diabetes
  • Lipid profile - dyslipidemia
  • Calcium and phosphate levels:
  • hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, myeloma, and renal disease
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone level:
  • hypothyroidism
  • Urinary uric acid excretion

Diagnosis #48

  • Skeletal x-ray films:
  • Gout
  • Kidney Ultrasound:
  • renal disease
  • uric acid kidney stones
  • Joint aspiration
  • diagnosis of acute gouty arthritis
  • uric acid crystals

Treatment #49

  • Asymptomatic hyperuricemia
  • Usualy good evolution
  • Lifestyle optimization : weight control, physical exercise, no alcohol, low-purine diet:
  • High in complex carbohydrates (fiber-rich whole grains, fruits, and vegetables)
  • Foods high in vitamin C (red cabbage, red bell peppers, tangerines, mandarins, oranges, potatoes)
  • Hydration - fruit juices and water (>8 glasses of water per day)
  • Low in protein (15% of calories and sources should be soy, lean meats, eggs)
  • No more than 30% of calories in fat (with only 10% animal fats)
  • Essential fatty acids (tuna and salmon, flaxseed, nuts, seeds)
  • To avoid : meats, poultry, fish, seafood, organ meats, alcohol, beans, and peas

Treatment #50

  • Symptomatic hyperuricemia - acute gouty arthritis
  • Initial goal is to provide symptomatic relief from pain
  • nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the drugs of choice for acute gouty arthritis
  • Colchicine - effective but used less frequently because of its adverse effects
  • intra-articular glucocorticoids
  • Lifestyle optimization (please see asymptomatic hyperuricemia)

Treatment #51

  • Chronic gout therapy
  • urate-lowering medication
  • uricosuric drugs (which promote uric acid excretion)
  • Probenecid, - inhibits the tubular reabsorption - increasing urate excretion
  • xanthine oxidase inhibitors (which inhibit uric acid production)
  • Allopurinol - competitive inhibitor of the enzyme xanthine oxidase.
  • acute lowering of urate levels can precipitate gout flare during the intercritical period. Thus, prophylactic colchicine coverage or low dose NSAID may be used.
  • Lifestyle optimization (please see asymptomatic hyperuricemia)

Treatment #52

  • Uric acid urolithiasis
  • Allopurinol
  • Increase the urine ph (6-7) to increase the solubility of uric acid
  • Potassium citrate, sodium bicarbonate or acetazolamide
  • Fruits, vegetables
  • Less meat, potatoes, rice, milk, cheese
  • Adequate hydration
  • Lifestyle optimization (please see asymptomatic hyperuricemia)

MALNUTRITION #53

Marasmus = energy malnutrition (negative energy balance). #54

  • Kwashiorkor = protein malnutrition, when the nitrogen balance is negative (less significant weight loss that can be masked by edema).
  • Pre- Cachexia = weight loss ≤ 5%, anorexia and metabolic changes.
  • Cachexia = weight loss> 5% or BMI <20 kg/m2 with weight loss> 2% or sarcopenia with weight loss> 2%.
  • Refractory cachexia = catabolic state unresponsive to treatment, with survival less than 3 months.

Slide 55 #55

Slide 56 #56

  • The degree of malnutrition (or undernutrition) in adults - assessed based on BMI: (kg/m²)
  • 17 – 18,4 - Grade I malnutrition
  • 16 – 16,9 - Grade II malnutrition
  • 13 - 15,9 - Grade III malnutrition
  • 10 - 12,9 - Grade IV malnutrition
  • < 10 - Grade V malnutrition
  • Types of malnutrition:
  • • Related to another condition, associated with inflammation: chronic diseases (cachexia), acute diseases
  • • Related to another condition, without inflammation
  • • Unrelated to another condition: psychosocial, socioeconomic factors, hunger

Slide 57 #57

Causes of malnutrition #58

  • Somatic: decreased appetite and taste perception, dental problems, dysphagia, gastrointestinal disorders involved in inadequate uptake, processing and absorption of nutrients, pain
  • • Functional: reduced mobility, asthenia, fatigue
  • • Psychological/psychiatric: anxiety, sadness, depression, cognitive impairment, anorexia nervosa
  • • Social: loneliness, poverty

Consequences of malnutrition : #59

  • • Decreased quality of life
  • • Increased risk for complications and infections
  • • Decreased functionality
  • • Decreasing the speed of wound healing, favoring the appearance of bedsores
  • • Increased risk of death
  • • Increasing the duration and costs of hospitalization

Clinical presentation #60

  • decreased fat deposits,
  • decreased muscle mass,
  • reduced mobility,
  • impaired memory and concentration,
  • asthenia;
  • amenorrhea (in women),
  • In protein malnutrition:
  • - skin abnormalities, hair loss, mucosal abnormalities, vasomotor dysfunction of the extremities, edema (by decreased intravascular osmotic pressure), infections (decreased antibody synthesis), delayed wound healing, neurological impairment

Biochemical: #61

  • Serum albumin reflects protein nutritional status in the last 1-2 months, with a half-life of 18-20 days. Levels may be falsely low in conditions of acute stress, hyperhydration, trauma, surgery, liver or kidney disease. False increases may occur in case of dehydration.
  • Serum albumin is not a good indicator of recent dietary changes (less than 3 weeks).
  • Significantly reduced serum albumin levels (below 3.5 mg / dl) have been associated in clinical trials with increased morbidity and mortality.
  • Serum transferrin - This parameter reflects the protein intake in recent weeks.
  • Severity criteria for malnutrition are weight loss over 10%, serum albumin below 30 g/l or lymphocytes below 1200/m3.

The nutritional intervention is adapted to the case and associated pathology #62

  • It has to be a gradual increase in caloric intake (over 30 kcal/kg/day in a week) and/or protein,
  • reduction in energy consumption (rest or light physical activity),
  • increasing the frequency of meals,
  • preparing tasty meals with a pleasant appearance .
  • Depending on the case, liquid or semi-liquid nutritional supplements, vitamin and mineral complexes are also administered.
  • Oral feeding is a priority, following the order of preference the enteral or parenteral route.
  • If oral intake is not sufficient, enteral/parenteral nutrition is considered (in hypercatabolic conditions, such as burns, extremely fragile nutritional status, significant digestive losses, reduced ingestion).

Protein-calorie malnutrition (PCM) #63

  • PCM is the most important nutritional condition in developing countries, especially due to its impact on infant growth, development and mortality.
  • In developed countries, PCM can be seen in the chronically ill patients, the elderly, hospitalized patients or people with disabilities. PCM can result from inadequate intake of protein, calories, or both.
  • Among the causes of PCM:
  • • Primary causes: insufficient food intake (caloric, protein), low quality protein intake, poverty, low supplies.
  • • Biological factors: malnutrition of pregnant women, infectious diseases.
  • • Environmental factors; unhealthy living conditions, improper food storage, calamities, wars.

Clinical aspects of PCM #64

  • • General signs: poor growth, reduced subcutaneous tissue, edema, muscle atrophy
  • • Skin: dry, scaly, exfoliative dermatitis, altered pigmentation
  • • Hair: friable, dull, depigmented or reddish
  • • Nails: cracked, with transverse striations
  • • Lips: cheilitis
  • • Tongue: atrophy of the lingual papillae
  • • Abdomen: distended, hepatomegaly
  • • Amenorrhea
  • • Fatigue
  • • Memory disorders

Nutritional interventions in protein-caloric malnutrition #65

  • The intensity and application of nutritional interventions in PCM is done depending on the severity.
  • In mild or moderate forms of PCM, resolving precipitating factors and increasing protein and caloric intake, depending on the current height in children and the ideal weight in adults, is considered sufficient. Supplementation of certain nutrients is only ensured if there are specific signs of deficiency of some of them.
  • The correction of these forms can be done in outpatient conditions, by ensuring a diet with easily digestible foods, energy dense, with high quality proteins and adequate micronutrients.
  • The objectives of the food intake are:
  • • doubling protein intake (from a recommendation of 0.8g protein/kg to 1.5g / kg) and
  • • 1.5 times increase in recommended caloric intake.
  • Severe cases of PCM are accompanied by increased mortality (40%), mainly due to infections, therefore it is recommended to care for these patients in the hospital.
